title: Git, dependencies and reproducible runs
objectives: Inspect working-tree changes and create an intentional source checkpoint without committing secrets.
Record and recreate a declared runtime/dependency setup while distinguishing isolation from reproducibility.
Apply git, dependencies and reproducible runs invariants safely and identify scope boundaries.
motivation: A useful result names the code and environment that produced it. Git records source snapshots; it does not automatically capture your Python runtime, database, untracked data or shell state.

blocks.md: A useful result names the code and environment that produced it. Git records source snapshots; it does not automatically capture your Python runtime, database, untracked data or shell state. Before committing, inspect git status and git diff. Add intended files explicitly, then inspect the staged diff with git diff --cached. Do not assume git add . is a safe default in a folder containing credentials or large generated data.

blocks.code:
git status --short
git diff
git add fee.py test_fee.py
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Test exact-cent fee contract"
blocks.caption: Illustrative commands for your own exercise repository after those files exist. Commit only intended files. Output depends on repository state; no fixed success output is claimed.

blocks.md: Keep tokens, passwords and private data out of source control. A .gitignore rule helps prevent accidental addition of currently untracked files; it does not remove a secret already tracked or erase it from history. If a credential was exposed, removing the file in a later commit is not enough: revoke/rotate the credential and follow the applicable incident procedure. No learner task here asks you to paste a secret.

A virtual environment isolates installed Python packages for a project. It is not a container or a complete machine snapshot. The same source may still behave differently across Python/library versions, OS/native libraries or external services. Record the versions actually tested and use a dependency manifest with appropriate version constraints or a lock process for the chosen tool.

blocks.code:
python3 -m venv .venv
# POSIX shell activation:
. .venv/bin/activate
python --version
python -m pip --version
# Use the project's reviewed dependency file if one is provided:
# python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
blocks.caption: Optional local setup. Windows activation differs. This module uses only the standard library, so installing third-party packages is not needed to run its examples. Commands may require local permissions and are not browser actions.

blocks.code:
import platform
import sys
print(sys.implementation.name)
print(platform.python_version())
blocks.caption: Prints the implementation and runtime version actually in use. The exact version is environment-dependent; it must not be memorised as a universal output.

blocks.md: A reproducible handover includes the source revision, run command, tested runtime, dependency resolution, input data/hash where appropriate, seeds and expected results with tolerances. Pinning package versions alone may not freeze transitive dependencies, platform wheels or external data. A seed does not guarantee identical output across every library version or parallel implementation. State the conditions under which you checked reproduction.

blocks.title: Boundary condition
blocks.md: Creating an environment does not install an uncached package while offline. These lessons remain readable offline; standard-library examples can be copied into a compatible local runtime. A browser code runner must explicitly report its capability and runtime availability rather than pretending a failed install is the learner's wrong answer.

Independent transfer: create a local exercise folder if you have Git/Python installed, save fee.py and its tests, inspect changes, run the tests and write a short RUN.md naming the command/runtime and synthetic input. If local tools are unavailable, inspect the supplied commands and identify which files/state a Git commit does and does not capture. The local-tool task is not a gate on reading the next lesson.

Technical references: [Git status](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-status) for status; [Git diff](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-diff) for working-tree and staged comparisons; [gitignore](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore) for the untracked-file scope and tracked-file limitation; [Python venv](https://docs.python.org/3.12/library/venv.html) for environment isolation. Reproduction and incident-handling tasks are declared engineering guidance, not claims that Git or venv captures a complete machine or handles exposed credentials automatically.

guidedExercise.prompt: What could still change after you pin direct package versions and a random seed?
guidedExercise.solution: Transitive dependency resolution, platform/native libraries, runtime, external data and parallel execution can differ. Record the conditions and compare the result against a stated tolerance.

options: Every untracked file, including ignored files
The changes staged for the next commit
Only the contents of a remote production database
All historical secrets and their revocation status
quiz.explanation: The cached/staged diff shows the changes staged in the index. Inspect it before committing intended source files. (This lets you inspect what the index will commit.)

quiz.prompt: What does a Python virtual environment directly provide?
options: A guaranteed identical copy of every external data source
A guarantee that every OS and CPU give identical numerical output
A substitute for recording the tested Python version
A project-specific environment for installed Python packages
quiz.explanation: A venv isolates packages around a Python installation. Full reproduction still needs source, runtime, dependencies, data and relevant platform assumptions. (It helps isolate package installations, not an entire machine.)

quiz.prompt: This Python module uses only the standard library. How many third-party packages must be installed just to run its worked examples?
quiz.explanation: No third-party package is needed for these examples. A compatible Python runtime is still required; zero packages does not mean zero runtime requirements.

quiz.prompt: A secret was committed yesterday. What does adding its filename to .gitignore accomplish?
options: It erases the secret from every historical commit
It revokes the credential at its issuing service
It does not remove a tracked secret or revoke it
It makes the existing secret safe to publish publicly
quiz.explanation: Ignore rules are not an exposure repair. A tracked secret can remain in history and the credential may remain usable until revoked. (Treat exposure separately and rotate/revoke as appropriate.)

quiz.prompt: Which handover best supports recreating a numerical result?
options: Source revision, run command, versions and input/seed assumptions
Only a screenshot of the final output number
Only the claim that it worked on one unnamed machine
Only a random seed, without code or library versions
quiz.explanation: Reproducibility needs enough information to recreate the checked conditions. A seed or screenshot alone does not specify them. (These record the conditions needed to repeat the checked run.)
